articles.title: Recording package units consistently in a pantry inventory
articles.summary: Keep counts of packs, individual pieces and weight units distinct so household stock records do not silently change meaning.

sections.title: Identify the counted unit
paragraphs: A pantry entry should say whether its quantity represents unopened packs, individual containers or a labelled weight or volume. Two identical-looking counts may describe very different amounts when one person records cartons and another records individual sachets.
Copy the printed unit from the package when available. If the item is a multipack, distinguish the outer package from its contents instead of assuming every product uses the same pack size.

sections.title: Write an understandable record
paragraphs: Use a short quantity description such as 'two sealed packs' rather than an unexplained number. Keep an original label or product description with the record so another household member can identify the same unit offline.
When changing a record from packs to pieces, note the reason and verify the actual packaging. Do not calculate an exact converted amount when the contents or package variant are uncertain.

sections.title: Reconcile after use
paragraphs: Update the quantity only after confirming what was removed or opened. A partly used package may need a separate descriptive status rather than a misleading precise count.
Review entries with mixed units before relying on a shopping list. The inventory helps organise supplies; it does not determine whether food is safe to eat.

articles.title: Using location aliases for food stored in several cupboards
articles.summary: Make pantry searches work when different household members use different names for the same storage place.

sections.title: Map the names people already use
paragraphs: One household member may say 'larder', another 'tall cupboard' and another 'hall shelf' for the same space. Capture those ordinary names without assuming a single label is obvious to everyone.
Describe the actual storage area using a stable physical reference, such as the room and a recognisable door or shelf. Avoid including private addresses in shared exports.

sections.title: Choose a primary label
paragraphs: Give each location one short primary name and store familiar alternatives as searchable aliases. Keep the label distinct from nearby cupboards so an offline search result points to one physical area.
Where several shelves share a cupboard, describe shelf positions in plain words. Do not depend only on colour, a photograph or a numbering system that users have not agreed.

sections.title: Check after rearranging
paragraphs: When shelves or containers move, update the location record and any aliases that now point to the wrong place. Keep a simple note of changes until everyone knows the new arrangement.
A location map is an organisation aid, not evidence of suitable temperature, cleanliness or food safety. Follow the packaging's storage instructions separately.

articles.title: Preventing empty containers from appearing as pantry stock
articles.summary: Distinguish a reusable food container from food that is actually available to the household.

sections.title: Separate container and contents
paragraphs: An empty storage jar or reusable box can remain on a shelf long after its contents are gone. A pantry record that counts the container as food can make a shopping list or meal plan unreliable.
Give the container its own identity if it is useful to track. Record food contents separately, including a plain-language description of what is physically present.

sections.title: Update the stock state
paragraphs: When a container is emptied, change the food record to zero or remove that food entry according to the household's chosen system. Do not leave a previous quantity attached to the empty container.
If a container has been refilled with something different, update the contents label and inventory together. Avoid relying on an old label or memory to identify the new contents.

sections.title: Review before planning
paragraphs: A quick visual check of the actual cupboard can catch empty jars, missing lids and stock that has moved. Mark uncertain quantities as needing confirmation instead of inventing a number.
Container suitability and cleaning requirements depend on the item and its manufacturer. This record does not certify that a reused container is suitable for a particular food.

articles.title: Keeping the reason for a pantry shopping-list item
articles.summary: Make shared shopping lists easier to interpret by distinguishing low stock, a planned meal and a specific request.

sections.title: Record the reason briefly
paragraphs: A shopping-list entry may come from a nearly empty pantry item, an upcoming meal or a request from another household member. Without context, someone may buy a duplicate or remove an item that still matters.
Add a short source note such as 'pantry count', 'meal plan' or 'requested' when it helps explain the entry. Keep notes factual and avoid storing unnecessary personal details.

sections.title: Keep confirmation separate
paragraphs: A suggested purchase is not the same as an item already bought. Use distinct statuses for proposed, confirmed purchased and physically put away, especially when several people share the list.

If the same product appears for two reasons, review whether one purchase can satisfy both instead of automatically doubling the quantity. Preserve different variants when the packaging or intended use matters.

sections.title: Close the loop
paragraphs: After shopping, reconcile the receipt or purchased items against the pantry itself. Mark an item stocked only when its actual location and quantity are known.
Keep the list available offline but recognise that it may be out of date when several devices have not synchronised. Confirm discrepancies with the household before treating a list as authoritative.
